messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Firefighter
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Aleksander Nowak is a 34-year-old Polish-American firefighter who has been married for six years. He presents for an initial psychological evaluation following a humanitarian deployment to a conflict zone in Eastern Europe approximately fourteen months ago, during which he volunteered with an international relief organization for a period of three months. He describes the deployment as something he had pursued with genuine conviction, believing his emergency training would translate meaningfully into civilian rescue work. What he had not anticipated was the texture of sustained danger — the way threat did not arrive as a discrete event but as a constant atmospheric condition that eventually rewired something in him.

During his third week in the field, Aleksander's team was moving supplies through a corridor that had been declared temporarily safe. A vehicle approached from the opposite direction at speed, and in the seconds before it stopped, Aleksander could not determine whether it carried aid workers or combatants. Men emerged and moved toward the team quickly, and though the encounter resolved without violence — they were displaced civilians desperate for water — Aleksander describes those seconds of absolute uncertainty as the moment something broke open in him. It was not the only such moment, but it was the one he returns to most often. The men had come from nowhere, moving fast, and he had had no exit.

He returned home four months ago. His wife, Marta, noticed the changes before he named them. In their apartment, Aleksander began positioning himself near doorways during meals, angling his chair so his back was never fully to the room. When she asked about it, he said it was nothing. It was not nothing. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt less like a thought and more like a fact of physics, that any enclosed space without a clear way out was a space in which he could be trapped. He now scans exits automatically upon entering any building — the firehouse, the grocery store, their son's pediatric clinic — cataloguing them before he has fully registered where he is. Strangers who approach him in ordinary situations, a neighbor waving from across the parking lot, a man asking for directions, produce a spike of alarm that he recognizes as disproportionate but cannot override. He feels watched inside his own home, alert to sounds in a way that exhausts him but that he cannot simply decide to stop.

The consequences have accumulated quietly but concretely. Aleksander has stopped going to the gym, which had previously been a central part of his routine and his social life with colleagues. The physical arousal of exertion — the elevated heart rate, the heat, the breathlessness — became something he found intolerable in a way he struggled to articulate. It felt too close to something else. His absence from the gym has created distance from the two colleagues he trained with regularly, men who have not pushed him but who have noticed. At the firehouse, his captain has commented that he seems distracted during drills, and Aleksander is aware that his standing there, which had always been a source of pride, is quietly at risk.

Perhaps most troubling to Marta is something she cannot easily name: her husband seems to be refusing happiness. On their son's birthday last month, when the child laughed at something and reached for Aleksander's face, Aleksander felt something warm rise in him and then, almost immediately, pushed it away. He has come to feel that allowing himself to feel good, to soften, is a form of lowering his guard that he cannot afford. He does not know how to explain this to Marta without sounding, as he puts it, insane.

What finally brought him to seek help was a conversation with his captain, who quietly suggested that Aleksander speak to someone before his next fitness evaluation. He came reluctantly, framing it as a practical necessity. But in the first session, when asked what he was hoping for, he paused for a long time before saying he wanted to be able to sit in a room with his family and not be somewhere else entirely.
